stories.title: Indigenous communities of Costa Rica and Panama
stories.subtitle: Rivers, coastal networks, settlements and ceremonial places before and around Spanish contact
stories.description: Rivers, coastal networks, settlements and ceremonial places before and around Spanish contact

scenes.title: A burial beside an ancient estuary
scenes.body: An adolescent was buried at Cerro Mangote in a place with an older history of gathering and preparing food.
scenes.note: The individual’s calibrated range is 2476–2293 BCE. Shorelines were different from the modern basemap.

scenes.title: Pottery below Las Mercedes-1
scenes.body: Deep sherds preserve a local history in the Caribbean foothills before the monumental center.
scenes.note: 800 BCE is a view into a broad typological horizon, whose early boundary is uncertain.

scenes.title: Meals on the Santa María River
scenes.body: Fish remains connect daily life at Sitio Sierra to both river and coast.
scenes.note: The food remains come from a dated refuse deposit, roughly 300–550 CE.

scenes.title: Postholes and terrace deposits
scenes.body: A posthole at Barriles Bajo and a stratified deposit at El Silencio show activity in two separate settings.
scenes.note: The date at El Silencio belongs to an early deposit. The large sphere’s placement remains undated.

scenes.title: Two cemeteries on the Río Grande
scenes.body: Richly furnished graves at Sitio Conte and El Caño preserve different histories of burial and offering.
scenes.note: This date falls within the published range for Burial 11 at Sitio Conte and the older of two calibrated windows at El Caño.

scenes.title: The places people built and used
scenes.body: Compare Guayabo’s waterworks and Las Mercedes-1’s plaza with everyday work on the Tárcoles and Isla Colón.
scenes.note: The selected evidence dates building phases, domestic activity, burial and settlement at different sites.

scenes.title: Entrances in the Diquís
scenes.body: At Finca 6 and Grijalba-2, paving and ramps shaped approaches to buildings above the floodplain.
scenes.note: One Finca 6 ramp context has a radiocarbon determination. Batambal and Grijalba-2 have broader architectural period assignments.

scenes.title: A former building becomes a burial place
scenes.body: People placed adults and children on and through a clay floor at Cerro Juan Díaz.
scenes.note: Four dated people provide the calendar envelope for this part of the settlement.

scenes.title: A new colonial port
scenes.body: The Spanish foundation at Panamá Viejo added a colonial settlement to a region already inhabited by Indigenous communities with long histories.
scenes.note: The colonial foundation is documented at this harbor. Earlier records across the region have their own kinds of evidence.

stories.title: Atlantic Brazil: mounds, villages and exchange
stories.subtitle: Coasts, rivers and local histories
stories.description: Follow coastal mound builders, river villages, pottery-making communities and the materials that connected them.

scenes.title: An early mound by a former lagoon
scenes.body: The builders at Rio Caipora accumulated shells near a lagoon on a coastline that has since shifted. Charcoal at the base preserves an early date for the mound.
scenes.note: The scene falls within the published basal charcoal calibration.

scenes.title: A burial mound beside an ancient bay
scenes.body: Chemical traces in the remains of people buried at Piaçaguera show that marine fish fed people who also used the land and freshwater environments around the bay.
scenes.note: Dated burials span a wider period and represent two overlapping groups.

scenes.title: Tools, food and small mounds
scenes.body: Morro do Ouro preserves a whale-bone harpoon component and independent evidence of varied diets. At Encantada III people covered a raised sand core with shell.
scenes.note: The scene intersects the published dates at both sites. Their purposes and histories differ.

scenes.title: Building on wet ground
scenes.body: People put a bed of thick shells over muddy ground at Amourins. On the Saquarema lagoon, Beirada’s layers preserve burials and work around hearths. Cabeçuda anchors a comparable period farther south.
scenes.note: Charcoal anchors construction deposits at Amourins. Shell and burial dates give their own local comparisons.

scenes.title: Reading the layers at Tarioba
scenes.body: Shells at Tarioba preserve evidence of how people formed the mound and how material shifted or mixed. Researchers have used that evidence to revise the site’s chronology.
scenes.note: The displayed span uses the outer bounds of the published start and end ranges.

scenes.title: A cemetery built through repeated gatherings
scenes.body: At Jabuticabeira II, people buried their dead, lit fires and covered older burial surfaces. Successive deposits joined to make a large mound.
scenes.note: The dates bracket several building episodes with uncertain boundaries.

scenes.title: Fish bone changes the face of a monument
scenes.body: Builders at Jabuticabeira II began using more fish-rich material in the upper deposits. Cabeçuda still received burials during the early centuries CE.
scenes.note: The original studies give broad calibration ranges for the shift and for the individual later burial.

scenes.title: Shell mounds and burials at Guanabara Bay
scenes.body: At Sernambetiba, people raised small shell mounds and then covered some with layers that joined them together. Excavators traced the buildup of shell, charcoal and fish bone and also found human burials at the site.
scenes.note: The viewing year lies within both calibrated charcoal ranges. The dates apply to sampled deposits at two depths.

scenes.title: Burials near the lagoons and the sea
scenes.body: A cremation near Una pottery on Ilha do Cabo Frio and charcoal inside a burial urn at Morro Grande preserve two ways coastal communities cared for their dead. The island deposits also held fishing and shell-working evidence.
scenes.note: 520 CE falls in the younger part of both calibrated ranges. Neither range fixes the year of a burial or establishes that the rites took place together.

scenes.title: Hearths between the coastal dunes
scenes.body: Near Jericoacoara in western Ceará, hearths, shell and retouched flakes survive in a dark layer between dunes. Nearby coastal outcrops supplied stone for tools.
scenes.note: Charcoal in the early layer dates to 424–583 CE. Separately dated deposits record later returns.

scenes.title: Different places by the same coast
scenes.body: Shell and bones accumulate beside Lagoa dos Freitas while people bury their dead at Içara and Galheta IV. The dune deposit can be compared with nearby funerary construction.
scenes.note: The dated intervals overlap. The archaeological deposits preserve different activities.

scenes.title: A tidal plain and a hill in the interior
scenes.body: At Zé Espinho, people built up shell deposits near Guaratiba’s rich fishing and gathering grounds. Inland, residents of Mata dos Bentes used clay pots with textured or painted surfaces and worked stone. The two places give different views of Indigenous life in the region.
scenes.note: 720 CE lies within the range for a burial context at Zé Espinho and a pottery age at Mata dos Bentes. The two dates come from different kinds of material.

scenes.title: Building on the Maranhão wetlands
scenes.body: At Formoso, people set wooden posts into a lake that flooded with the seasons. Post-built settlements also stood in the Pericumã and Turiaçu basins. The lakes and rivers gave people places to fish and waterways to travel.
scenes.note: Calendar windows come from separate pieces of wood and, at Formoso, soot on pottery. The posts can be younger than the dated portions of the trees.

scenes.title: A greenstone pendant at Boca do Rio
scenes.body: People at Boca do Rio built a long central structure surrounded by smaller clusters. Cooking vessels and finer pottery suggest different uses for those spaces. A small greenstone pendant found in the center was made from a stone with no known Maranhão source.
scenes.note: The date comes from a wooden pile. The pendant is an associated find, with its source and means of transfer unresolved.

scenes.title: Clay vessels from Alagoas to western Bahia
scenes.body: Potters on the Serra da Barriga made vessels used in daily life and in burial. At Praça de Piragiba, people laid their dead in pear-shaped urns with ceramic lids, often grouped together. At Alcobaça, people used a sandstone shelter for burial and other activities.
scenes.note: The evidence is a dated sherd, a dated urn burial and a different directly dated burial in the rock shelter.

scenes.title: Pottery, worked stone and a cemetery
scenes.body: Caçapava 1 preserves an urn cemetery in the Paraíba Valley. In the Zona da Mata, fired vessels and worked stone accumulated on hills at Primavera and Poça. Dated features and artifacts place these communities at several distinct places in the interior.
scenes.note: 1200 CE falls within the early urn date from Caçapava 1 and the early pottery ranges at Primavera and Poça.

scenes.title: Urns and rock-shelter burials
scenes.body: Excavations in Ceará recovered clay burial vessels at Serra do Evaristo and a large painted bowl used for a secondary burial at Baixio dos Lopes. In the Pernambuco Agreste, marks on one individual's bones show how his remains were prepared for burial.
scenes.note: These records come from different communities and directly dated or associated contexts. Several assays have gaps between their calibrated intervals.

scenes.title: Cooking vessels beside the lagoon
scenes.body: At Riacho dos Franciscos II, absorbed residues in Guarani-style pottery provide evidence of maize processing. Galheta IV supplies a nearby comparison for late coastal practices.
scenes.note: The dated Riacho context applies to the locality. The sampled sherds preserve different uses of the vessels.

scenes.title: Hearths in the eastern interior
scenes.body: Charcoal and pots from Córrego do Maranhão record work at different places on a ridge. At Rio Preto Oeste in Espírito Santo, soot-covered ceramics, a reused urn and combustion features preserve traces of village life above a river. Teixeira Lopes and Emílio Barão add evidence from nearby hills in Minas Gerais.
scenes.note: 1375 CE intersects calibrated charcoal and pottery ages in Minas Gerais and the provisional fourteenth-century assignment at Rio Preto Oeste.

scenes.title: Household ground and burial vessels
scenes.body: Two fifteenth-century charcoal samples date work in different parts of Santa Marina. Dark patches of earth there preserve the debris of everyday life. People at Caçapava 1 buried their dead in urns, and a much broader charcoal range records the possible later use of a burial area at Morro Grande.
scenes.note: 1420 CE lies within the two Santa Marina calibrations, the later Caçapava 1 window and the broad age of the later Morro Grande hearth.

scenes.title: Graphite for the potters of Canaã
scenes.body: Potters beside the Rio Colônia added graphite to their clay and also used it to coat vessels. A comparison with mineral samples makes the Jequié area a possible source for some of the graphite.
scenes.note: The line relates a candidate source area to the find locality. A separately dated graphite-coated sherd provides the age context.

scenes.title: Two burials at the edge of the dated window
scenes.body: Shell pendants and painted bowls accompanied a woman buried at Bananeiras. At Arapuan, people buried an individual in the upper part of an older shell mound. The graves reveal different ways coastal people cared for their dead. Either burial could belong to the colonial period.
scenes.note: The recent Bananeiras calibration starts at 1500 CE. An earlier calibration allows a late fifteenth-century date. Arapuan’s date also extends into the colonial period.

stories.title: After Lapita in the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu
stories.subtitle: Shoreline villages, gardens, shrines and voyages from the first millennium BCE to 1800 CE
stories.description: Shoreline villages, gardens, shrines and voyages from the first millennium BCE to 1800 CE

scenes.title: Nenumbo’s reef-side hamlet
scenes.body: Bananas appear in excavated soils at a Lapita hamlet near a former lagoon on Ngaua.
scenes.note: The sample envelope expresses dating uncertainty for an occupation archaeologists understand as much shorter.

scenes.title: Mounds and pots in Vanuatu
scenes.body: Shell, pots and cooking stones accumulated at Mafilau as people tended plants and gathered coastal foods. Pottery at Matantas shows activity on the north coast of Santo.
scenes.note: Both markers refer to sampled archaeological contexts.

scenes.title: A village outside the cave
scenes.body: Te Ana Tavatava grew from a cave locality into a village. Repeated layers of coral gravel record the upkeep of house floors.
scenes.note: The range marks the excavators’ broad estimate of village use.

scenes.title: Pots followed different histories
scenes.body: People at Lamen, Melarip and Sinapupu used forms of pottery with distinct histories and regional affinities.
scenes.note: Lamen has a dated shell context. The Melarip sherds are dated by style.

scenes.title: Stone drains at Ivanaud
scenes.body: Along the Anetcho River, farming left buried stone-lined drains in valley-floor sediments.
scenes.note: The early age is from a correlated exposure beside the river.

scenes.title: Changing tools and ritual places
scenes.body: On Tikopia the beginning of Tuakamali is visible in a change of tools and ceramics. Around the same time, people were building a stone-faced shrine at Bao.
scenes.note: The scenes align approximate age windows from separately studied places.

scenes.title: Distant stone in village deposits
scenes.body: Dating from village deposits puts imported Tutuila adzes on Taumako and New Britain glass on Sikopo in the same broad period.
scenes.note: Chemical provenance places the source of each material. The intermediate stops remain unknown.

scenes.title: Walls and relations across islands
scenes.body: Stone walls framed Mangaas yards and enclosed shrines on the Roviana ridge. On Emae, imported obsidian from the Banks Islands was discarded in a midden.
scenes.note: The historic properties, excavation settings and samples provide separate windows.

scenes.title: Mobility remembered at Namu
scenes.body: Tooth enamel from people buried at Namu points to movement among islands during their lifetimes.
scenes.note: The marker dates the sampled burial population. The individual journeys took place earlier.
